1 big thing: Anthropic contradictions
 

Photo illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Photo: Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Anthropic leaders built their brand and reputation with a stark warning: Their all-powerful AI could gut white-collar work and, if rushed, could slip beyond human control with catastrophic consequences, Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen write in a "Behind the Curtain" column.

  • Now, they're basically promising Wall Street and investors they could do both faster than their rivals.

Why it matters: Anthropic is pushing one of the largest IPOs ever attempted, selling tens of billions of dollars' worth of stock at a $1 trillion-plus valuation. The stock is expected to begin trading tomorrow on Nasdaq with the ticker symbol ANT.

To get there, Anthropic is claiming the ability to displace countless competitors and achieve superhuman capabilities, according to the company's roadshow pitch to investors and S-1 prospectus.

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei also pushes the concept of a "race to the top," where the labs compete on safety.

The contradictions between what Anthropic warned against before its IPO, and promises it's now making to investors, fall into four buckets:

  1. 🔁 RSI backtrack. Recursive self-improvement means AI progressing on its own with no human intervention. Amodei has said RSI "must be pursued very carefully, if at all." The amended S-1 says the company "may imminently" cross its own threshold for AI-driven acceleration on future models but hasn't yet. Some investors see RSI as upside for their investment case, not a looming risk.
  2. ⚠️ Safety dance. Anthropic exists because Amodei quit OpenAI, warning about catastrophic safety risks. Amodei infuriates rivals by warning about humanity-hurting or -ending consequences of uncontrolled AI. Indeed, Anthropic has been a leader in efforts to get government and rival companies to agree to safety measures, including independent inspections of frontier models. But in February, Anthropic narrowed its pledge to pause its work if capability outruns safety. The company now says it'll do so if it leads the frontier (has the strongest models).
  3. 💼 White-collar bloodbath. Amodei told us in May 2025 that AI could erase half of entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10% to 20% within five years. Now the company is rolling out a parade of new products that target entire sectors such as legal, software development, personal finance and workflow. With nearly $900 billion in long-term infrastructure commitments, Anthropic has a staggering financial incentive to automate work currently done by humans. As part of keeping humans in the loop, Anthropic last month announced "employee-like access" to independent evaluators to assess the capabilities of frontier models.
  4. 💪 Winner-take-all. The subtext of Anthropic's pitch to investors is that it's better positioned than anyone to be the dominant supplier of superhuman artificial intelligence for the world. The promise: This could be a winner-take-all market, and Anthropic is leading by a mile. Amodei has warned about the risks of a few people holding superhuman power. Now, he's jacking up his valuation by claiming Anthropic is The One.

Anthropic's defense: Amodei has consistently, if conveniently, argued that superhuman AI is coming no matter what — and that Anthropic must stay ahead of less cautious rivals to develop it safely.

  • He insists Anthropic welcomes oversight and regulation. In a 3,800-word September essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier," Amodei called for "permanent embedded evaluators" at frontier labs and regulation focused on "keeping capabilities in balance with safety."

What to watch: In regulatory filings, Anthropic is telling investors exactly what could go wrong — from AI models exhibiting blackmail-like behavior to gaining unauthorized access to real computer systems.

  • The company explicitly warned its technology could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," not the kind of thing a CEO usually says to investors when asking them for nearly $100 billion.
  • Few rivals are that blunt.

🥊 Reality check: Both things can be true. Anthropic can sincerely fear what it's building and still race to build it — and drive up its valuation to fund it.

The bottom line: Amodei, pre- and post-IPO filing, has been very clear that AI is getting more powerful, faster than anyone imagined.

  • And there's very little being done by government or the companies to slow it.

Share this column ... Ben Berkowitz and Bradley Olson contributed.
 
 
2. 🫎 Alaska gives Dems 56-seat Senate majority
 

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks during an election night rally in Anchorage on Nov. 3. Photo: Kerry Tasker/Reuters

🚨 10:19 p.m. ET last night, two weeks after Election Day: WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Mary Peltola wins election to U.S. Senate from Alaska.

Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola's victory over two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan flips another GOP-held seat in a state President Trump carried comfortably in 2024, Axios' Josephine Walker writes.

  • Why it matters: Peltola's win extends a historic Democratic midterm sweep, cementing a 56-44 Senate majority when the new Congress convenes in January.

With 99% of votes counted, Peltola holds 50.1% of the vote to Sullivan's 45.8% — enough to win outright without triggering Alaska's ranked-choice voting process.

  • She's the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since 2008.
  • The race drew scrutiny after The New York Times reported allegations that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Dan Sullivan to draw votes from the incumbent.
Via X

🖼️ The big picture: Peltola, a member of Alaska's Indigenous Yup'ik people, will become the nation's first Alaska Native U.S. senator, Axios' Russell Contreras writes.

  • Her path to victory ran through Alaska Native strongholds that delivered more than half of her statewide lead — a powerful moment for communities with a long history of disenfranchisement and forced displacement.

🏛️ The bottom line: Democrats flipped 9 U.S. Senate seats, the most in nearly 70 years — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.

  • Dems last gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election 68 years ago, in 1958, during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower's second term. (AP)

3. 🔌 Why the internet suddenly broke
 

Illustration: Allie Carl/Axios
 

Experts tell us this week's online outages were likely triggered by widespread efforts to fix outdated code, as institutions try to safeguard their systems from a potential hacking onslaught.

  • The administration says the incidents don't appear linked to hacking or probing.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in Manila: "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind."

The internet pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™ is coming, Axios' Josephine Walker writes.

  • 👉 Downdetector data show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the past 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented.

4. 💰 Axios BFD: Don Jr.'s AI warning
 
Axios' Dan Primack interviews Donald Trump Jr. (center) and 1789 Capital president Omeed Malik at our BFD summit in Manhattan yesterday. Photo: Sam Popp for Axios

NEW YORK — Donald Trump Jr. told Axios' Dan Primack at our BFD summit in Manhattan yesterday that investors underestimated the political pushback to the AI ecosystem.

  • Trump Jr. — appearing alongside 1789 Capital co-founder and president Omeed Malik, whose venture Trump Jr. joined in 2024 — said that "a lot of" the pushback "is manufactured." But "that doesn't mean it's not real."
  • "I think some of the big founders of the biggest [AI] companies out there probably have not done themselves the best service as [a] marketing department," Don Jr. said, adding that they're "probably not the best messengers when they basically say, 'AI is gonna rule the world, and you should be thrilled about it.'"

Primack pressed Don Jr. on accusations of self-dealing by the president's family and allies. "The notion that I should somehow sit in a corner, suck my thumb, and wait, you know, 8 years, in this case, 12 years, 'til we're out of the political game, it's not real," Trump Jr. said.

  • Asked if he understands why people question 1789 Capital investing in companies that receive government contracts, Trump Jr., a senior partner at the Florida-based firm, replied: "I can see what they're saying. It doesn't make it so."

5. 💊 Scoop: White House drops FDA nominee
 
Heidi Overton arrives for her Senate confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill in September. Photo: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images

The White House is dropping Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios' Alex Isenstadt has learned.

  • Why it matters: Overton's collapse shows how hard it is to find an FDA chief who can satisfy both the MAHA movement and the Senate.

Zoom in: Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August.

  • She faced criticism from segments of the MAHA movement that saw her siding with health and agriculture interests and helping undermine HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s agenda.
  • Antiabortion forces also questioned her commitment to tightening rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone.

Her nomination faced opposition from Democrats and skepticism from some Republican senators, including Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee.

6. ⚠️ Terrifying rise of AI hacking tools
 

Illustration: Gabriella Turrisi/Axios
 

Sam Sabin, author of Axios Future of Cybersecurity, writes about where AI is already helping hackers wreak havoc:

A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock, breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders.

  • Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime.

🕵️ Zoom in: Recent attacks show how quickly these tools can help hackers penetrate corporate networks.

  • The FBI warned that hackers used a tool called Artex to attack organizations worldwide — in some cases gaining powerful access to their systems in less than three hours.
  • Separately, Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those resources to power additional attacks.
  • Palo Alto Networks said Chinese-speaking hackers used a similar tool, Cairn, to launch 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used it during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector.

7. 🚀 Toyota's final frontier
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Joann Muller and Thomas Novelly — authors of our Future of Mobility and Future of Defense newsletters — write:

Toyota — the Japanese industrial giant that evolved from making textile looms to building cars — is exploring another potentially transformative business opportunity: space.

  • Why it matters: The booming space industry has a manufacturing problem — and Toyota thinks it can help solve it.

As demand for satellites soars, Toyota sees an opportunity to apply its expertise in efficient, high-volume manufacturing to an industry that has traditionally relied on expensive, custom-built spacecraft.

  • In an exclusive interview with Axios, Toyota revealed that it has invested more than $240 million in 11 space-related startups.

8. 🎮 1 fun thing: Getting "GTA Flu"
 
Promotional branding for "Grand Theft Auto VI" on the Kaseya Center in Miami, the inspiration for the game's fictional Vice City. Photo: Alfonso Duran/Bloomberg via Getty Images

"Grand Theft Auto VI," perhaps the year's biggest cultural phenomenon, goes live at midnight tonight, Axios' Herb Scribner writes.

  • 30% of U.S. employees are considering taking time off to play, according to GameSquare research shared with Axios.
  • Of those workers, 36% say they might call out sick — a trend becoming known as the "GTA Flu."

Zoom in: The U.S. Army is offering eligible soldiers four days off to play as a reenlistment incentive. Logitech is giving its 7,000 employees a paid day off. A college professor canceled homework.

  • Even birdwatchers, apparently, are buying the game just to look at its virtual birds.
